utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: A very good morning to everybody. And thank you for coming this early, by all means. Let's go immediately, medias in res. May I ask you, Madam Registrar, to please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. This is case number IT-01-42-A, the Prosecutor versus Pavle Strugar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And may I have the appearances of the parties? For the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Helen Brady appearing on behalf of the Prosecution. Together with me today are Mr. Xavier Tracol and Ms. Michelle Jarvis and our case manager Ms. Lourdes Galicia. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And for the Defence, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. On behalf of the Defence team, Goran Rodic and Vladimir Petrovic, attorneys at law as counsel for Mr. Strugar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And I have to ask you, Mr. Strugar, can you hear me and the parties, and can you follow the proceedings in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry, but I couldn't follow. Once again, you can follow the proceedings in a language you understand, Mr. Strugar? Thank you. You may be seated again and now ... As you know, the purpose of a Status Conference is to allow a person in custody, pending appeal, the opportunity to raise issues in relation thereto, including the health situation and, if any, complaints about detention conditions. Mr. Strugar, do you wish to raise any such issue?

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no complaints to make about the conditions in the Detention Unit. As far as my health is concerned, considering my age, it is quite difficult and there are a number of ailments I am troubled by. But I wish to thank you for the understanding you exhibited with regard to my hip operation, which was fully successful. However, it seems that they will have to operate on my left hip as well. Then there is my prostate and dementia, which troubles me the most, as well as my rheumatism. But at any rate, my physician at the Detention Unit is fully informed of my condition and I take my medications regularly. But I have no complaints or issues to raise, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Strugar. May I ask Defence counsel, do you want to add anything in this direction?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Very briefly, I would like to draw your attention to several circumstances the Defence deems important at this stage. First of all, on behalf of the Defence, I would like to thank the Pre-Appeal Judge and the entire Appeals Chamber for having enabled our client recently to be taken good care of in the Medical Health Centre in Podgorica to deal with his hip. What I would like to point out is that the health condition of General Strugar in the recent months, and one could even say years, is continuously deteriorating. The number of ailments he suffers from is constantly present and steadily increasing. As Mr. Strugar himself pointed out just now, his health problems are numerous. The first and foremost is the difficulties he suffers from his kidneys that are quite impaired, and as far as we know, only with the adequate medical treatments can this condition be remedied. His prostate also poses a daily problem for him. Dementia and the mental state of Mr. Strugar in general is something that impairs his memory faculties, which are, in his case, quite highly impaired. There are a number of other difficulties he's faced with that I can inform the Appeals Chamber of in a different form, however. I wish to say that, given Mr. Strugar's age, his present situation in the Detention Unit is such that, in our view, constitutes a very heavy burden for him. His condition requires adequate medical care at all times. He has that sort of medical care in the Detention Unit, but he requires a very complex, all-encompassing medical care that is to be provided in a propitious environment. Besides, his family situation is quite complex as well. His wife, who is of an advanced age as well, is unable to visit him here because of, among other things, her eyesight difficulties. Her eyesight is impaired by 90 per cent. She is almost blind and, for this reason, cannot visit him at the UNDU. Given the numerous difficulties, ailments, Mr. Strugar's age and his specific family situation, General Strugar, after serving the sentence to which this Appeals Chamber will convict him to, can have at least a few years of, let's say, quality life, if he were to serve his sentence in an environment that would enable him to have constant medical care and constant contacts with his family. In our view, such medical care could be provided to General Strugar only if he were to serve his sentence in one of the institutions in Montenegro, the country he hails from. In this regard, the Defence respectfully appeals to this Chamber to be of assistance in this matter and, if possible, to inform Mr. Strugar's Defence of their view as to whether there is the possibility, in the context of this Tribunal's Statute, Rules of Procedure and Evidence and other legal acts, in view of the very specific circumstances of this case that are quite different from other cases that were before this Tribunal, for Mr. Strugar to serve his sentence in one of the relevant facilities in the territory of Montenegro. Furthermore, the Defence would like to hear the view of the pre-appeals Judge with regard to such a possibility. Finally, I would like to say that the Defence is aware of the fact that when it comes to the discussion about the facility to be determined for such a purpose, the Defence would be prepared to withdraw their notice of appeal, or appeals brief, in order to make this sentence final; that this would be, of course, the precondition for such a discussion. Therefore, we would first like to know whether, legally speaking, there is the possibility for such an option, which, in our opinion, would be the best solution for the situation in which Mr. Strugar currently finds himself. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I thank you. I think we have two separate issues before us. One is the health situation and the second is how to continue. Do you have any medical certificates on the actual health situation of Mr. Strugar, preferably a holistic overview of the entire health situation?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the latest documents we have concerning Mr. Strugar's health are the documents which date from the period when Mr. Strugar was provisionally released in Podgorica. The documents are comprehensive and cover different aspects of his health condition. We don't have one single document, but all these documents cover all the aspects of his health problems that I have just talked about. Unfortunately, we don't have documents that would date from this recent period after his return to the UNDU, but we would be able to obtain it as soon as possible, just as we are prepared to offer all the documentation we already have for your perusal as well as to the other side, of course, in these proceedings. The documentation is quite extensive. It is in existence and can be placed at the disposal of the Appeals Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask you when can this documentation be submitted to the other party and to the Bench?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in 10 days' time, at most, I believe we would be able to prepare the documentation for you and for the other party. As the documentation is already in existence, we would be able to do it sooner. However, there is the issue of having the documents translated. Therefore, the time that we require in this respect is the time that is necessary for a good translation of the documentation. Given the nature of the documents, the documents cannot be translated but by the interpreters who have the adequate expertise. That would be the time limit we require. Of course, we would wish to do it sooner, but we do not want to be in a situation to have to even take longer than the time limit you impose us. That is the time we think we require.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So if I take your answer together, we can expect the documentation in one of the Tribunal's official languages no later than, say, not the next but in the following week, Monday, would this be correct, already translated?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. We will make all efforts to make sure that it is ready by next Friday. Maybe Monday. We will try to do this as soon as possible, but it will be ready by the Monday that you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. And this will be the absolute deadline because we have to proceed with the case. Now let's turn to the second issue you raised, the question of enforcement. As you correctly highlighted, this matter is not before the Appeals Chamber. We have to deal with the appeal presented by both parties, and the question of an enforcement arises only when a decision has become final. You alluded to the possibility that there might be a withdrawal of your appeal. I have to ask the Prosecution on its position later on. But before I do so, I have to emphasise that the power to finally decide on enforcement arrangements is vested in the President of the Tribunal, pursuant to Rule 103(1) of the Rules and pursuant to the practice direction of the determination of enforcement states. According to these norms, the Registrar, in consultation with the President, would first have to conclude agreement with the Government of the Republic of Montenegro to that effect, and the prison conditions in Montenegro would have to fulfil the standards required by the Statute, the Rules and the relevant United Nations provisions and principles. Thus, as a Pre-Appeal Judge, I'm not authorised to decide on this matter. As it is not the first time that we've discussed Mr. Strugar's wish to have his sentence enforced in the Republic of Montenegro, I have carefully reviewed the legal situation and, personally, I do not see any general obstacle to give a strong recommendation to both the Registrar and the President to grant, if there should be a mutual withdrawal of both appeals and therefore the sentence has become final, the conviction has become final, to grant such a motion for humanitarian reasons based on the health situation of Mr. Strugar. But this, of course, depends on the documentation you are prepared to submit soon. In case there is -- in fact, I have, as I said, to ask the Prosecution as well to mutually and at the same time withdraw your respective appeals. I have to submit this to the entire Bench, which has to decide whether or not to accept such withdrawals as being informed, voluntary and unequivocal ones, and to order, if need may be, final dispositions pursuant to Rules 101(C) and 103(C) of the Rules. Because the question already is in the room of a withdrawal, in particular from the side of Defence - and this is a personal matter for Mr. Strugar - I have to stress that such a notification, under no circumstances, can be revoked. Therefore, I have to re-emphasise that I'm not able to give any guarantees. What I can do and what I will do if such a situation arises is to give a strong recommendation based on humanitarian grounds that Mr. Strugar may serve the remaining part of his sentence in his home country. But let us hear the Prosecution on this.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, the Prosecution takes no position on the enforcement of the sentence. This is a matter, as Your Honour has said, for the Registrar together -- the President together with the Registrar. But we have heard today that Mr. Strugar would be prepared to withdraw his appeal against a trial judgement, and based on the -- what we would call the exceptional humanitarian circumstances pertaining in this case, especially in relation to his advanced age and poor state of health and general condition, based on Mr. Strugar's preparedness to withdraw his appeal, the Prosecution is likewise prepared to consider its position in relation to its own appeal in this case and, in particular, whether to withdraw its appeal in this case. And I stress again that this is based on the special humanitarian considerations in this case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I thank you. We have no doubt to proceed with the case, either based on a mutual withdrawal, as indicated now by both parties, or we have to proceed with the hearing of the appeal as such, as soon as possible. But as I already stressed in a prior Status Conference, this will not be possible in any event this year. So it is first for the Defence to demonstrate the health situation, and on this basis I have to submit all the documents and the entire situation to the Bench. But as I don't want to have another Status Conference soon, and as there is an urgent need to know how to proceed, please understand that I expect a final decision from both parties no later than by the end of the -- not the next but the following week. Otherwise, we have to conclude the discussion on whether or not to withdraw appeals, but then we have to proceed on the appeal as such. As this is the only possibility to hear Mr. Strugar right now whether he has understood all these proceedings and whether maybe his decision to withdraw the appeal is an informed one, may I ask you, Mr. Strugar, did you understand all the proceedings, in particular, that I'm, by the Rules --

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe I have understood. As far as I'm concerned, and as far as my personal decision is concerned, I join the attitude of my Defence. We've discussed this matter in front of you, Your Honour. May I remind and reiterate that my psychological status, not regarding this process but my age, ever since I arrived to the Tribunal to face up to my responsibility, I've been the oldest detainee. On the 13th of July, I turned 73, and because of the natural processes going on in my organism, I very much differ from other inmates. They are predominantly aged 30 to 40; maybe one or two in their 50s. Our mindset, as individuals, is very different. I myself realise, and this bothers me, I tend to forget things. There are certain situations where I'm -- I find myself in very embarrassing positions. And if I were to look back at my reactions with hindsight, I realise that it was my guilt as well. We have different mindsets. The others inmates are too young for me, and I'm too old to understand their behaviour. That's one thing. The other thing is that my professional background and history means that, from very early on, I had to meet much stricter criteria to behave more -- in a more civilised or cultured way. I'm not only bothered by the behaviour of the young people, I am positively offended by it. But it's not their fault, it is my fault that at such an advanced age I have to find myself in such circumstances. So as far as what my Defence counsel related to you, I fully agree. It would mean much to me to be in an ambience or environment which would be different from the present one. As he stated, my wife is only one year my junior. She lost one eye. She had two surgeries on the other eye; first due to glaucoma and the second time due to cataracts. So she is almost blind. The people in this courtroom have seen my wife visiting me. So all the psychological pressure on me, because I do speak to her on the phone, is too much to bear. So I personally would like to ask you to consider the possibility, in a humane way. I know that it's very difficult to ask for anything but your human understanding. These are my thoughts about the situation. The people around me do not understand me, and this is very hard for me. People are what they are. I cannot change them. Thank you very much for your patience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. When you started, I was just about to say that you're the -- if any, your decision has to be an informed one. You have heard that neither I nor the Chamber as such can give any guarantees at this point in time because the power is clearly vested in the Registrar and finally the President. Once again, you have fully understood -- you have fully understood that once you have taken a decision, the decision cannot be revoked?

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT
utterances.text: Yes. [Interpretation] I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Are there any other submissions to be brought to our attention? I can so none. And therefore, I can only repeat that I expect the documentation as soon as possible on the health condition; however, no later than the 15th -- the 10th of September, and the final decision of both parties no later than mid-September, on or about the 15th of September, because we have to proceed in one or the other direction. I think it would be helpful, if there is such a situation from your side, that you would, at the same time, file the withdrawal -- a withdrawal of the appeals, and then it's, as I said, submitted to the entire Bench and finally to the Registrar and President. And let's hope that at the end of the day, even though we have a serious case of infringement of humanitarian law before us, that nevertheless humanity may prevail. I thank you for today, and I hope this was the last Status Conference in this case.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the Status Conference adjourned at
